To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

action-inaction framing leads to higher escalation of commitment than inaction-action framing (i.e., the inaction effect), and that this effect is mediated by the inaction-effect tendency to take action in the presence of negative feedback.
action-inaction framing leads to higher escalation of commitment than inaction-action framing, and this framing effect is mediated by inaction bias.
action-inaction framing of the escalation-de-escalation decision leads to higher escalation of commitment to a losing course of action.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of framing on escalation of commitment, and it contributes to the literature on escalation-of-commitment research by offering a new perspective on escalation and by showing how framing influences the escalation-decision process
a new inaction-effect perspective on the sunk-cost fallacy and the tendency to escalate commitment to a course of action.
the role of inaction framing and negative feedback in the escalation of commitment to a losing course of action.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
action-inaction framing increases escalation of commitment to a greater extent than action-inaction framing.
action-inaction framing leads to higher escalation of commitment in the presence of negative feedback.
framing escalation as inaction and de-escalating as action leads to higher escalation of commitment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
negative feedback results not only in the tendency to act but also in a tendency to take the action that is most easily available.

framing escalation-decisions in a way that emphasizes the action component of escalation leads to a stronger escalation tendency than framing in a way that de-emphasizes the action component of the de-escalation option.

negative feedback results not only in the sunk-cost fallacy, which is the tendency to escalate in the presence of sunk costs, but also in the action-inaction fallacy, which occurs when people are action oriented and thus tend to escalate, even in the absence of sunk costs.
